task: Check a cable diagram against CDP. Display the brief neighbor table containing SW1’s local interfaces and the peers’ advertised ports.

teaching.hint: Keep the command’s local device separate from the neighboring device.
teaching.takeaway: Local Intrfce belongs to SW1; Port ID belongs to the advertising peer. Verify the reverse observation before correcting the diagram.

task: On an LLDP-capable IOS switch, display the brief received-neighbor table to compare local and remote port IDs with the diagram.

teaching.hint: Use the protocol the peer actually advertises.
teaching.takeaway: Read this table’s own capability legend: LLDP B denotes bridge. The displayed remote port ID belongs to the peer, not to the switch where you ran the command.

task: The brief CDP table identifies a neighbor but omits the management-address detail you need. Display detailed records for all current neighbors.

teaching.hint: Expand the received neighbor records, not the local interface configuration.
teaching.takeaway: Read whichever addresses the peer actually advertises. A listed address is not a successful reachability test and does not authenticate the neighbor’s identity.

task: The brief LLDP view omits the chassis and management details needed to resolve a neighbor identity. Display all received neighbor details on this supporting image.

teaching.hint: Use the expanded LLDP neighbor view.
teaching.takeaway: Compare chassis ID, port ID and system name; those identifiers may have different formats. Optional management fields can be absent without making the advertisement invalid.

task: CDP has been disabled globally on SW1. Re-enable its device-wide process while retaining existing per-interface exclusions.

teaching.hint: Global process state and interface permission are separate controls.
teaching.takeaway: The global process must run before permitted interfaces participate. This does not override an interface explicitly configured not to use CDP.

task: A compatible non-Cisco neighbor uses LLDP. On this LLDP-capable IOS image, enable SW1’s global LLDP process.

teaching.hint: Enabling Cisco’s other discovery protocol would not enable LLDP.
teaching.takeaway: Required interfaces still need appropriate transmit and receive settings. A running global process alone does not establish that a neighbor has been learned.

task: The selected SW1 interface faces an unmanaged boundary where CDP is prohibited. Disable CDP only there, preserving internal discovery.

teaching.hint: Use an interface-scoped change rather than stopping the global process.
teaching.takeaway: Other interfaces can continue CDP. LLDP is a separate protocol and retains its own transmit and receive settings.

task: On the selected SW1 link, stop advertising SW1 through LLDP but keep SW1 able to receive the peer’s advertisements.

teaching.takeaway: The peer stops receiving fresh SW1 advertisements; its cached record may remain temporarily. SW1 can still learn the peer if the opposite transmit and local receive settings permit it.

task: On the selected SW1 link, stop learning incoming LLDP information while leaving SW1’s outgoing advertisements enabled.

teaching.takeaway: SW1 stops refreshing peer information on this link. The peer may still learn SW1, and old cached entries need not disappear immediately.

task: CDP runs globally, but an expected neighbor is missing. Display local CDP interface participation to check whether the intended port is enabled for discovery.

teaching.hint: Check the local protocol interface state before blaming IP routing.
teaching.takeaway: This shows local participation, not proof of a received peer advertisement. Then check the far end, physical state and record freshness.
